- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.75) and forecast shows a sharp upward spike, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment turns negative (≤ -0.33) and forecast is still rising, cut the forecast slope early to prevent overcorrection.  
- In periods with strong mean reversion signals (sentiment swings sharply), model should not overfit recent highs; cap forecast at 1–2 standard deviations above recent mean.  
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), avoid overreacting to short-term volatility; use 3–5 day smoothing on forecast adjustments.  
- If forecast consistently overestimates early in the 30-day horizon (e.g., first 5–7 days), apply a 3–5% downward bias to correct for lagged momentum.  
- In high-sentiment environments, forecast should not exceed 1.5x the 18-day moving average unless sentiment is explicitly bullish and sustained.  
- If sentiment is consistently negative and forecast is still rising, treat as “false breakout” — reduce forecast by 10–15% from peak.  
- For multi-day sentiment shifts, adjust forecast slope to match sentiment trend direction, not just magnitude.  
- Avoid forecasting below 65% of 18-day moving average unless sentiment is clearly bearish and confirmed.  
- If forecast and true outcome diverge by >10% in first 3 days, re-evaluate sentiment signal strength — if sentiment is weak, reduce forecast volatility.
